title: Match and project
idea: `$match` keeps only the documents that pass a filter. `$project` decides which fields each document carries on.
points: `$match` uses the same filter syntax as `find()`.
Put `$match` first, so later stages handle fewer documents.
In `$project`: `1` keeps a field, `0` drops it, `_id` stays unless `_id: 0`.
Set a field to an expression, such as `'$customer'`, to rename or compute it.

left.title: $match
items: Passes on only documents that satisfy the filter
Output: fewer documents, each one unchanged
Cannot add, rename or remove fields

right.title: $project
items: Keeps, drops, renames or computes fields
Output: the same documents in a new shape

code.title: Filter, then reshape
code.caption: Two pipelines on the shared data. Step through them, then press Run.

walk.text: Keep paid orders from Porto, using the filter syntax `find()` takes.
`_id: 0` hides the id. Without it, `_id` comes back.
`total: 1` keeps a field. `name: '$customer'` copies another field under a new name.
An expression computes a new field: here, how many items the order has.
`$sort` runs after `$project`, so it can only use fields kept or created there.
Exclusion form: with only `0` values, every other field stays. Here `items` and `_id` go.

pitfalls: Do not mix `1` and `0` in one `$project`; only `_id: 0` may be mixed.
A stage after `$project` sees only the fields you kept.
A misspelt field in `$match` is not an error; it matches nothing.

quiz.why: `$project` kept only `customer`, so `status` no longer exists when `$match` runs. No document passes.

takeaway: `$match` picks documents, `$project` picks fields; match first.
